archetype.name: Bubble Team (run-and-gun)
archetype.definition: Anaheim is a high-event club that outscores its problems with an elite power play and finishing, while losing at 5-on-5 and getting bottom-tier goaltending, which leaves it hovering around a playoff line it hasn't clearly earned.

report.headline: A power play and hot sticks are covering for the league's leakiest crease
report.take:
Anaheim at 11-9-1 looks like a mid-table team, and by goal differential it is one: 79 scored, 77 allowed, sixteenth in Goal Diff / GP. But the line is extreme at both ends. The Ducks score 3.76 a game (5th) and allow 3.67 (29th). Few teams score this much, and few give up this much.

The offense runs through four forwards and a power play converting at 35.2%, best in the league and 13 points above the average. Cutter Gauthier has 18 goals, Beckett Sennecke 12, and Leo Carlsson's 27 points include 17 on the power play. The team's all-situations shooting percentage is 14.7%, second in the league, against a league mark of 11.4%. The split between the two PDO figures shows where that comes from. At 5-on-5 the Ducks' PDO is 99.3, below average. In all situations it is 101.2. The hot finishing is a special-teams story, not an even-strength one. At even strength they are a 46.3% xGF team (26th) on a 50% Corsi share. They have the puck plenty, but they create less dangerous looks than they give up.

The goaltending is the core problem, and it isn't new. The team save percentage is .865, 31st, and Goalies GSAx is -5.2. Lukas Dostal has started 11 games at .856 with -5.1 GSAx on his own, and the group grades an F. Last season the Ducks also finished 29th in Def Rank with -12.8 GSAx. This is a second straight year of the crease giving goals away, not an early-season wobble. Shots against are actually decent at 26.5 a game (12th). Combine that with the weak xGF share and the picture is a team that allows a moderate number of shots, too many of them good ones, and then doesn't get the saves.

The November surge was 6-2, with 4.5 goals a game. That run was mostly a 5-1 shootout stretch, not a defensive fix: they still allowed 3.38 a game. The 90-point pace almost exactly repeats last season's 92. That's a fair read on the next few months unless one of three things changes. The power play could cool, which is likely to some degree. Dostal could find his game, which is possible. Or the 5-on-5 chance share could improve, which needs more than this roster has shown.

strengths.title: League-best power play
strengths.body: The Ducks convert 35.2% of their power plays, first in the league and well clear of the 22.2% average. Carlsson, Gauthier, LaCombe, Sennecke and Granlund each have double-digit PP points, so the unit isn't leaning on one hot shooter. Nobody holds a rate like this all season, but the personnel is real. Expect it to settle closer to very good than elite.

strengths.title: Top-four forwards can finish
strengths.body: Gauthier (18 goals on a team-high 87 shots) and Sennecke (12 goals, 26 points) both rank 6th on their wing tabs, with Carlsson and Granlund close behind at center. Those four carry a B forward grade and the 5th-ranked offense, despite a team that ranks only 26th in shots per game. Second-in-the-league shooting will cool, but Gauthier's shot volume gives him a sturdy floor.

strengths.title: Luneau steadies the back end
strengths.body: Tristan Luneau is the one defenseman winning his minutes, with a .552 xGF share. He ranks 17th on the defense tab and plays 20 minutes a night. Jackson LaCombe's 22 points are mostly offense, while his .382 xGF share in 26.9 minutes shows the top pair is bleeding chances. Giving Luneau more of the hard matchups is the obvious lever.

concerns.title: Goaltending is giving games away
concerns.body: A .865 team save percentage ranks 31st, 2.7 points below the league average, and the group grades an F. Dostal has started most games and accounts for almost the whole -5.2 GSAx. Last season's -12.8 makes this a pattern, not a slump, so a rebound to average can't be assumed.

concerns.title: Losing the 5-on-5 chance battle
concerns.body: A 46.3% xGF share ranks 26th, down from 51.9% last season. Every forward-position line against them runs well above expectation: forwards score 1.42 points a game more than their averages predict, 30th in the league. That is partly bad goaltending, but the chance share says the defensive structure is also to blame.

concerns.title: Special-teams finishing will cool
concerns.body: The gap between a 99.3 5-on-5 PDO and a 101.2 all-situations PDO puts the hot shooting on the power play. A 35.2% conversion rate is not a stable number. When it drops, an offense that ranks 26th in shots per game has little volume to fall back on. The 74.1% PK (22nd) doesn't offset the swing.

trend.note: A 5-8 October gave way to a 6-2 November, and the last ten games went 6-3-1 at 4.7 goals a game. The rise is offense-driven: in that stretch they allowed more per game than their season average.

weekAhead.headline: Four road games, two soft penalty kills, one Avalanche wall
weekAhead.body:
All four games are on the road, and the opponents vary widely. St. Louis is the hardest test for how Anaheim scores: an 84.6% penalty kill (8th) and a .904 team save percentage (7th) behind B+ goaltending. The Blues barely score themselves (26th Off Rank), though, which gives a leaky Ducks crease some slack. Colorado is the real problem. Its A+ forward group drives a 2nd-ranked offense and a 52.9% xGF share, exactly the kind of attack that punishes Anaheim's 5-on-5 weaknesses and its goaltending.

The back half is friendlier. Utah's penalty kill sits at 70.4% (27th) and its goalies post a .869 save percentage (30th), so the Ducks' power play should feast. Utah also controls play with a 56.8% xGF share and owns the league's 2nd-best power play, so expect a track meet. Seattle ranks 29th on the site, with a 62.7% kill (31st), a 41% Corsi share (last), and a 30th-ranked defense that is especially generous to wingers. Coming out of the trip with five or six points is a realistic target.

keyMatchups.title: Ducks PP vs Utah and Seattle kills
keyMatchups.body: The league's best power play meets two of its worst penalty kills, Utah 27th and Seattle 31st. Draw penalties in these two games and the special-teams edge should decide them. This is the week's clearest advantage.

keyMatchups.title: Colorado's forwards vs Ducks' crease
keyMatchups.body: Colorado has an A+ forward group, the 2nd-ranked offense, and 30.2 shots a game. Anaheim's goaltending grades an F with a .865 save percentage. Unless Dostal or Brossoit steals one, this is the game most likely to get away.

keyMatchups.title: Gauthier and Sennecke vs Seattle
keyMatchups.body: Seattle gives up 4.39 points a game to wingers, and wingers take a .459 share of the points against it versus a .381 league norm. Anaheim's two best goal scorers are both wingers. That sets up a big night for the top line in the finale.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts in net and what he stops: Dostal's .856 against St. Louis and Colorado will say more about this team's ceiling than any scoring line.

restOfSeason.body:
The likeliest path is a season much like last year's: a high-scoring team in the high 80s to low 90s in points, on the bubble of the Pacific race. Edmonton and Vegas are already pulling ahead, and Seattle and San Jose are close behind. The offense should stay top-ten because the top four forwards are legitimate. The power play and team shooting percentage will drift down, though, and the 26th-ranked shot volume means scoring dips when they do. The defense shouldn't get much worse: a .865 save percentage is near the floor, and some recovery toward the league's .892 is plausible even from a below-average tandem.

What the sheet doesn't support is a breakout. The 5-on-5 chance share has slipped from last season. The goaltending has now been below expected for two years. Pts vs Goal Diff is slightly negative, so there's no hidden close-game luck to give back, but there's no hidden cushion either. I'd project about 84 to 94 points. The top of that range requires Dostal to return to average.
swingFactors: Dostal's save percentage moving toward league average
How far the power play falls from 35%
Whether the 5-on-5 xGF share climbs back toward last year's

confidence.note: 21 games is a modest sample, but the goaltending and defensive problems match last season.
